title: The Man of God from Judah and the Old Prophet
summary: A man of God from Judah interrupts Jeroboam's worship at Bethel and prophesies that a Davidic king named Josiah will burn the bones of priests on that altar; the altar splits and the king's hand withers and is restored. Commanded not to eat or drink there, the man refuses the king's hospitality but is deceived by an old prophet of Bethel into returning, and on his way home a lion kills him. The old prophet buries him in his own tomb, and Jeroboam goes on in his sin.
story: Jeroboam has just built his own altar at Bethel (12:32-33). Before the incense has finished burning, God answers with a word from Judah, from the south, where the house of David and the temple remain. The oracle reaches three centuries ahead to King Josiah, whose reforms in 2 Kings 23:15-18 fulfill it in detail, even sparing the tomb that holds both prophets. The strange second half of the story turns the spotlight from the king to the prophets themselves: the word of the LORD is so serious that even its messenger is not exempt from obeying it. The chapter closes by returning to Jeroboam, who learned nothing, and names his sin as the reason his house will be destroyed.
historical:
The setting is the early reign of Jeroboam I, about 930 to 910 BC, at the royal sanctuary of Bethel. Josiah reigned in Judah from about 640 to 609 BC, and 2 Kings 23 records that he tore down the Bethel altar, burned bones from the tombs on it, and left the bones of the man of God and the old prophet undisturbed, just as this chapter anticipates. The phrase the cities of Samaria in verse 32 is notable, since the city of Samaria was not founded until Omri's reign (16:24). Many interpreters take it as the narrator's later name for the northern territory, used from the vantage point of the book's final editing.

The naming of Josiah centuries in advance is read in different ways. Traditional interpreters take it as genuine predictive prophecy, one of a handful in which a future ruler is named (Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28 is another). Many critical scholars think the name was added or sharpened when the history was compiled in or after Josiah's day. Both views agree that the book of Kings presents the Bethel altar as condemned from its founding.
cultural:
In the ancient world, sharing a meal created a bond of fellowship and obligation. The man of God's command not to eat or drink in Bethel was an acted sign: he was to have no fellowship with a place under God's judgment, and not even to return by the same road, as though the place could not be touched twice. The king's offer of a meal and a reward was an attempt to bring the prophet under royal patronage and so blunt his word.

The title man of God was a common way to describe a prophet, a person sent with God's message. There were many prophets in Israel, some genuine and some not, and hearers had to weigh their words. The old prophet's claim that an angel spoke to him appeals to a higher authority to overrule a clear command. A lion killing a traveler was a real danger in the land in this period, but the lion that kills and then stands still beside the body and the donkey, eating neither, is a sign that this death was a judgment, not an accident. Burying a stranger in one's own family tomb, and asking to be buried beside him, was an act of deep honor and solidarity.
literary: The chapter is a carefully shaped prophetic story with two halves that mirror each other. In both, someone invites the man of God home to eat (verses 7 and 15), and in both he repeats the command he received (verses 9 and 17). The difference is the lie of verse 18. Key words tie it together: the word of the LORD occurs again and again, and the verb return (shuv) and the noun way keep appearing, so that the question of which road to take becomes the question of whether to obey. The ending is ironic. The lying prophet becomes the one who speaks the true word of judgment (verses 20-22), and the man of God who defied the king's power falls to a lion. The frame (verses 1-10 and 33-34) keeps the reader's eye on Jeroboam, who witnessed signs and still did not turn.

outline.t: The man of God cries out against the altar at Bethel
The king's hand withers and is restored
The man of God refuses the king's hospitality
The word of judgment and the lion on the road
The old prophet buries the man of God

doctrines.note: The word of the LORD drives the whole chapter: it condemns the altar, gives a sign, binds the messenger, and comes true centuries later. A clear word from God is not overturned by a later claim of revelation that contradicts it.
Judgment falls on the disobedient prophet in the short term and on Jeroboam's house in the long term. The chapter insists that closeness to God's work raises, rather than lowers, accountability.
Jeroboam saw his hand wither and be healed, and the altar split, yet he did not turn from his evil way (verse 33). Signs alone do not produce repentance; a heart must return to God.

words.note: Shuv, to turn or return. The man of God must not return by the way he came, he is brought back, and Jeroboam does not turn from his evil way (verse 33, where the same verb means repent). The one word links the story of the road to the question of repentance.

Derekh, way or road. It is literally the road the man of God travels, and it is also the Old Testament's common word for a manner of life. His death on the road, and Jeroboam's evil way, show the two meanings meeting.

Kachash, to deceive or lie. The narrator states it flatly: the old prophet was lying to him (verse 18). The text gives no motive, and interpreters have guessed at jealousy, testing, or a wish to share in the man of God's honor.

christ: The oracle against the Bethel altar looks forward to a son of David who will purify worship, and Josiah is that king in the book's own story. Kings shows, though, that Josiah's reform could not save Judah from exile (2 Kings 23:26-27), so the longing for a son of David who would cleanse worship at its root remains. The Gospels present Jesus acting in that role when he drives the traders from the temple, and he teaches that true worship is in spirit and truth, not tied to a rival sanctuary (John 4:21-24). The chapter's hard lesson about false prophets also runs into the New Testament, where Jesus warns against false prophets and Paul says that even an angel from heaven preaching a different gospel is not to be believed (Galatians 1:8). These are thematic links rather than predictions of Christ in the text.

hard.q: Why did the man of God die for being deceived, while the lying prophet lived?
hard.a:
This is one of the most troubling stories in Kings, and the text does not fully explain it. Several things are clear. The man of God had received a direct and specific command, and he had repeated it twice; the old prophet offered only a claim of a later message, which contradicted what God had already said. The story treats a prophet's obedience to his own commission as a matter of life and death, because the whole point of his mission was that Bethel was a place with which God's messenger could have no fellowship. By eating there, he undid the sign he had been sent to be.

The liar is not excused. He is exposed as a liar, becomes the unwilling mouth of judgment, and ends grieving and asking to be buried beside the man he betrayed. Interpreters differ on his motive, and the text leaves it unstated. What the story presses on its readers is that God's word must be weighed against what he has already clearly said, even when it comes from someone who claims to be a prophet.

questions: The man of God stood firm before a king but gave way to a fellow believer. Why can pressure from a trusted person be harder to resist?
How do you weigh a new claim about what God wants against what he has already clearly said?
Jeroboam saw undeniable signs and did not change. What keeps people from turning even when they know they should?
